title: Λῃστὴς καὶ συκάμινος
titleEn: The Robber and the Mulberry Tree
part: The Robber and the Mulberry Tree (Chambry 214)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 214. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λῃστὴς ἐν ὁδῷ τινα ἀποκτείνας, ἐπειδὴ ὑπὸ τῶν παρατυχόντων ἐδιώκετο, καταλιπὼν αὐτὸν ᾑμαγμένον, ἔφευγε.
sentences.tr: Lēistēs en hodōi tina apokteinas, epeidē hypo tōn paratychontōn ediōketo, katalipōn auton hēimagmenon, epheuge.
sentences.l: A robber, having-killed someone on the road, when he was-being-pursued by those who happened-to-be-there, having-left him blood-smeared, was-fleeing.
sentences.i: A robber killed a man on the road, and when the passers-by gave chase he left him bloodied and ran.
sentences.n: οἱ παρατυχόντες, "those who chanced to be present", is the ordinary Greek for bystanders. ᾑμαγμένον is a perfect passive participle of αἱμάσσω, to make bloody — the state the body is left in, and the state the robber's own hands are in.

sentences.t: Τῶν δὲ ἀντικρὺς ὁδευόντων πυνθανομένων αὐτοῦ τίνι μεμελυσμένας ἔχει τὰς χεῖρας, ἔλεγεν ἀπὸ συκαμίνου νεωστὶ καταβεβηκέναι.
sentences.tr: Tōn de antikrys hodeuontōn pynthanomenōn autou tini memelysmenas echei tas cheiras, elegen apo sykaminou neōsti katabebēkenai.
sentences.l: And those travelling in the opposite direction asking him with what he has his hands stained, he was-saying that he had-come-down from a mulberry tree just now.
sentences.i: When those coming the other way asked him what had stained his hands, he told them he had just climbed down from a mulberry tree.
sentences.n: Another genitive absolute (τῶν ὁδευόντων πυνθανομένων), with τίνι a dative of means, "by what". ἔχει with the perfect passive participle and τὰς χεῖρας says he has his hands in a stained condition — the standing state, not the act of staining. The form as Chambry prints it is μεμελυσμένας; the expected participle of μολύνω, to defile, would be μεμολυσμένας, and the reading here is odd — it is left as printed. The mulberry's juice stains a deep red, which is what makes the lie a good one.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὡς ταῦτα ἔλεγεν, οἱ διώκοντες αὐτὸν ἐπελθόντες καὶ συλλαβόντες ἀπό τινος συκαμίνου ἀνεσταύρωσαν.
sentences.tr: Kai hōs tauta elegen, hoi diōkontes auton epelthontes kai syllabontes apo tinos sykaminou anestaurōsan.
sentences.l: And as he was-saying these things, those pursuing him, having-come-up and having-seized him, from a certain mulberry tree hanged him up.
sentences.i: Even as he was saying it, his pursuers came up, seized him, and hanged him on a mulberry tree.
sentences.n: ἀνασταυρόω is to fix a man on a stake — to impale, and in later usage to crucify; with ἀπό and the tree it is a hanging from its branches. The tree he named for his alibi becomes the instrument of his death, and the fable says so without comment.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ ἔφη πρὸς αὐτόν· « Ἀλλ’ ἔγωγε οὐκ ἄχθομαι πρὸς τὸν σὸν θάνατον ὑπηρετοῦσα· καὶ γὰρ ὃν αὐτὸς φόνον ἀπειργάσω, τοῦτον εἰς ἐμὲ ἀπεμάττου. »
sentences.tr: Hē de ephē pros auton· « All’ egōge ouk achthomai pros ton son thanaton hypēretousa· kai gar hon autos phonon apeirgasō, touton eis eme apemattou. »
sentences.l: And she said to him: « But I for my part am not vexed at serving toward your death; for the murder which you yourself wrought, this you were-wiping-off onto me. »
sentences.i: And the tree said to him: « I am not grieved to be of service to your death; for the murder you did yourself, you were wiping off onto me. »
sentences.n: ἡ συκάμινος is feminine, so the sentence opens simply Ἡ δέ, "and she" — tree names in Greek are regularly feminine, and no noun is repeated. ἀπομάττομαι is to wipe something off oneself onto another, and the metaphor is exact here, the blood transferred to the tree's juice. ἀπειργάσω and ἀπεμάττου are second person singular middle, aorist and imperfect: the killing done once, the wiping-off going on.

sentences.t: Οὕτω πολλάκις καὶ οἱ φύσει χρηστοί, ὅταν ὑπ’ ἐνίων ὡς φαῦλοι διαβάλλωνται, κατ’ αὐτῶν πονηρεύεσθαι οὐκ ὀκνοῦσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtō pollakis kai hoi physei chrēstoi, hotan hyp’ eniōn hōs phauloi diaballōntai, kat’ autōn ponēreuesthai ouk oknousin.
sentences.l: Thus often even those good by nature, whenever they are slandered by some as base, do not shrink from playing the villain against them.
sentences.n: ὅταν with the subjunctive is the general condition, "whenever", stating a rule and not one occasion. φύσει is a dative of respect, "in their nature". The moral reads the tree as the innocent thing pushed into complicity: the robber laid his own stain on it, and it was content to be the instrument of his end.
